summary: The note describes the tapetum lucidum, a retroreflective tissue behind the retina found in many vertebrates and some other animals, which boosts night vision by reflecting light back through the retina at the cost of slight blurring. It covers the four structural classes of tapeta, the eyeshine effect and its colors, how eyeshine is used by humans to identify animals in the dark, artificial retroreflectors inspired by it, and drug-induced pathology in dogs.
one_line: Overview of the tapetum lucidum, the retroreflective eye layer that boosts night vision and produces eyeshine in many animals.
key_facts: The tapetum lucidum is a layer of tissue lying immediately behind the retina that acts as a retroreflector.
The tapetum lucidum reflects visible light back through the retina, increasing the light available to photoreceptors although slightly blurring the image.
In the cat, the tapetum lucidum increases the sensitivity of vision by 44%.
Haplorhine primates, including humans, are diurnal and lack a tapetum lucidum.
The tapetum lucidum cells are leucophores, not iridophores, though the tapetum is iridescent like other iridescent tissues.
Nathan H. Lents proposed that the tapetum lucidum evolved in vertebrates but not in cephalopods because of the backwards-facing nature of vertebrate photoreceptors.
The note lists four classes of tapeta: retinal, choroidal guanine, choroidal tapetum cellulosum, and choroidal tapetum fibrosum.
Choroidal tapetum cellulosum is seen in carnivores, rodents and cetacea; dogs and ferrets use zinc, cats use riboflavin and zinc, and lemurs use only riboflavin.
Choroidal tapetum fibrosum is seen in cows, sheep, goats and horses, and consists of an array of extracellular fibers, most commonly collagen.
Nightjars use a retinal tapetum lucidum composed of lipids.
In tigers the tapetum lucidum is greenish, and the color in reindeer changes seasonally.
White eyeshine occurs in many fish, especially walleye; blue eyeshine occurs in horses; green eyeshine occurs in cats, dogs and raccoons; red eyeshine occurs in coyote, rodents, opossums and birds.
Blue-eyed cats and dogs may display a distinctive red eyeshine in flash photographs, independent of the eyeshine from the tapetum.
Most spider species have a tapetum located only in their smaller lateral eyes, and the salticids (e.g. Salticidae) have no tapetum.

In dogs, drugs including ethambutol, macrolide antibiotics, dithizone, antimalarial medications, some H2-antagonists and cardiovascular agents can disturb tapetum crystal organization and impair low-light vision.
The earliest artificial retroreflector patent, used in 'Catseye' brand raised pavement markers, was inspired by the tapetum lucidum of a cat's eye.

entities.name: Tapetum lucidum
entities.role: layer of tissue behind the retina that acts as a retroreflector and boosts night vision in many vertebrates

entities.name: Nathan H. Lents
entities.role: American scientist who proposed the tapetum lucidum evolved in vertebrates but not in cephalopods

entities.name: Catseye
entities.role: brand of raised pavement markers whose early patented design was inspired by the tapetum lucidum of a cat's eye

entities.name: Brownsnout spookfish
entities.role: fish that has an extraordinary focusing mirror derived from a retinal tapetum

entities.name: Aotus
entities.role: neotropical night monkey genus sometimes described as having a tapetum of collagen fibrils but lacking riboflavin crystals

entities.name: Eulemur
entities.role: lemur genus with several diurnal species among otherwise nocturnal strepsirrhine primates
